newsitem.title: JAPAN: Parties in new Japan alliance announce platform.
newsitem.headline: Parties in new Japan alliance announce platform.

text.p: The three parties in Japan's outgoing ruling coalition agreed to set up a loose alliance on Thursday, meaning Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto will likely form a minority government.

They also announced policy goals, including reforms of the powerful Finance Ministry and bureaucrats in general, but stopped short of renewing their formal ties, meaning Hashimoto's government could be toppled in a no-confidence motion should his allies decide to support the opposition.

"Things have greatly changed since the coalition under (former prime minister Tomiichi) Murayama," Social Democrat leader Takako Doi said after signing the documents in a meeting with Hashimoto and Akiko Domoto of the Sakigake party.
"The shape of the government will be different. This is what I said during the meeting," Doi said.
Hashimoto's Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) failed to win a majority in the October 20 Lower House election and tried to renew the coalition that first put him in power last January.
But the Social Democrats and Sakigake, both which lost heavily in the polls, refused, saying they feared becoming irrelevant partners in a grouping dominated by the LDP.
The LDP won 239 seats, 12 short of a majority, while the Social Democrats won 15 and Sakigake two.
In place of the coalition, the three parties agreed to keep a loose, out-of-government alliance by setting up policy consultation groups outside the cabinet, Doi said.
The two parties will not have members in a new Hashimoto cabinet to be formed on November 7 after his scheduled re-election as prime minister.
Though short of a majority, Hashimoto is assured of his re-election because of the LDP's strength in parliament.
The new alliance means Hashimoto will in effect lead a minority government, which could easily be toppled in a no-confidence motion should his allies decide to support the opposition.

The joint policy platform issued on Thursday includes a reaffirmation of former Prime Minister Tomiichi Murayama's war apology of 1995 and calls for the further reduction of U.S. military bases on Okinawa, which houses more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan.
Proposed reforms include a plan to set up an organ to oversee banks and other financial institutions separate from the powerful Finance Ministry and give more independence to the central bank.

The alliance also agreed to draft a reduction of the central government's 20 ministries by next year and set up parliamentary committees to review the tax system and to oversee the conduct of bureaucrats.
But the parties failed to agree to ban political donations from private firms, something anathema to the LDP which has survived on funds from the big businesses.

The LDP also rejected Social Democrat demands to begin formal talks with the United States to reduce the actual number of troops on Okinawa. About 20,000 U.S. military personnel, including an entire Marine Corps division, are stationed there.

It remained to be seen whether the policy platform will act as a strong bond cementing the alliance or be used as a pretext to quit the alliance if the LDP reneges on any of the stated promises, political analysts said.

LDP officials said they would start policy negotiations with the Democrats, a new party comprised of a younger generation of reformists headed by outgoing Health Minister Naoto Kan, and with a five-member group of independents who have said they would vote for Hashimoto on November 7.
However, the Democrats and the independents have said they would not join in a coalition.
